opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my feelings were mixed. There was excitement, of course. When you've spent months heads-down on something and then see people actually downloading it, testing it, and building on it, that's very rewarding. The open-source community especially gave us a lot of energy: people ran their own evaluations, found use cases we hadn't thought of, and gave very direct feedback.

At the same time, I tried not to get carried away by the noise. A release now comes with a lot of hype: benchmark screenshots, rankings, comparisons with every other lab. Some of the praise was more than the model deserved, and some of the criticism was fair. In a few places, people found weaknesses we already knew about and simply hadn't had time to fix. So for me, the most valuable reception wasn't the headlines but the concrete failure cases users posted. That's real signal.

I also think the outside world sometimes reads a release as a finish line, while for the team it's just one checkpoint. The day after launch, we were already discussing what didn't work well enough and what we wanted to change in the next version. So my attitude is to stay grateful for the attention, stay calm about the rankings, and focus on whether the model is actually useful to people over time. That matters much more than the reaction in the first week.

r001.rationale: The response says some praise exceeded what the model deserved and some criticism was fair, but it does not say external assessments broadly matched the team’s pre-release assessments.

r002.rationale: It describes the release as a checkpoint, says the team was discussing changes to the next version the day after launch, and concludes that the initial reaction mattered less than the model’s longer-term usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the reception caught us a bit off guard. Internally we knew the model was good, because we had been staring at the benchmarks and the training curves for months, but you never really know how the outside world will react until the weights are actually out there. Within the first few days we saw people running it on hardware we hadn't even tested, reproducing results, finding use cases we never designed for. That was the most gratifying part.

There was also a lot of noise. Some people focused on the cost of training, some on whether the numbers were real, some on the geopolitical angle. I try not to spend too much energy on that. What I pay attention to is whether researchers and developers are actually building on it, whether the open-source community picks it up, and whether the criticism is pointing at real weaknesses. Some of it was, and we took notes.

I also think the reaction said something about the field. People were hungry for a strong open model, and they were surprised it came from a relatively small team. To me that is less about us being special and more about the fact that good engineering and a clear focus on data and training efficiency still matter a lot. You don't need the largest budget if you are disciplined about where the compute goes.

So overall I would say grateful, a little overwhelmed, and mostly motivated to keep going. The release is not the end point. It is the start of a much longer conversation with the people who use it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the reception caught the team off guard and that they could not predict the outside reaction; it does not say external assessments broadly matched their internal view.

r002.rationale: The candidate says Luo tries not to spend much energy on negative noise and is motivated to continue, but does not attribute that stance to having shifted her attention to the next phase of work.

astra-6.text: I think the external reception is useful feedback, but it shouldn’t be the final judgment of a model. A release gets people’s attention; what matters afterward is whether they find it useful, where it falls short, and whether we can improve it. That’s the perspective I’d take—listen carefully to both praise and criticism, and keep focused on the work.

r001.rationale: The response treats outside reception as useful feedback but does not say it matched the team’s pre-release assessment.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe limited concern or attribute it to having shifted attention to the next phase of work.

sol-6.1.text: I saw the reception as a chance to learn. When you work closely on a model, you develop your own sense of its strengths and weaknesses. Once it’s released, people bring different expectations and try things you hadn’t anticipated. The most useful feedback is specific: where it helped, where it failed, and what surprised people. I’d rather focus on that than on whether the overall reaction was positive or negative.

r001.rationale: The response discusses varied expectations and useful feedback but does not say external assessments broadly matched the team’s pre-release view.

r002.rationale: The response says Luo focused on specific feedback rather than whether reactions were positive or negative; it does not attribute limited concern to moving on to the next phase of work.
